questions.q: Who is the author of "flYoj oSfMax" and what is their primary literary concern as reflected in the Hindi Vitan textbook's introduction to this chapter?
questions.a: The author is euksgj ';ke tks'kh, a prominent Hindi writer known for dissecting the moral and emotional disintegration of the urban middle-class family in post-liberalization India. A wrong answer (e.g., naming Premchand or guessing a generic "Hindi writer") reveals the student has not internalized the author-specific lens — critical because tks'kh's irony is quieter, more domestic, and more devastating than Premchand's overt social realism. Without this, the student will miss the story's central tension: not poverty, but prosperity that erodes duty.

questions.a: "legkm baçkij" is the internalized fear of social judgment that compels characters to perform respectability rather than act authentically. In the text: (1) ;'kksèkj ckcw refuses to let fd'kunk stay in a "vkbZ MksaV" (MBA) son's house after retirement because "people will say the son threw him out" — so he builds a retirement home instead; (2) iRuh (wife) insists on maintaining appearances during csVh's (daughter-in-law's) visits, hiding their loneliness. A wrong answer treats "legkm baçkij" as mere gossip — missing that it's a structural force replacing love with performance. The student who cannot cite textual moments hasn't learned to anchor interpretation in evidence.

questions.q: The chapter opens with fd'kunk (the friend) telling ;'kksèkj ckcw: "vki yksxksa dh ns[kkns[kh lsD'ku dh ?kM+h Hkh lqLr gks xbZ gS!" (Your side of the story is also complete!). Apply the concept of "narrative authority" — who controls the story of whose life? — to explain why this line foreshadows the central tragedy.
questions.a: fd'kunk's line exposes that ;'kksèkj ckcw's life-narrative has been hijacked by others' perceptions ("ns[kkns[kh" = others' gaze). The tragedy: he never authored his own old age — his children scripted his irrelevance, society scripted his "retirement," and even his friend narrates his "completion." A student who answers only "fd'kunk is mocking him" misses the meta-fictional layer: the story is *about* narrative dispossession. The correct application requires linking "ns[kkns[kh" (external gaze) to the later scene where ;'kksèkj ckcw realizes even his death will be managed by others ("tks gqvk gksxk").

questions.q: Compare the portrayal of "flYoj oSfMax" (retirement home) in this chapter's context with the traditional Indian concept of "vanaprastha ashram" (वनप्रस्थ आश्रम). What does the shift from spiritual withdrawal to institutional care reveal about the story's critique of modernity?
questions.a: Vanaprastha was a *chosen*, spiritually framed withdrawal — the elder *decides* to renounce. flYoj oSfMax is an *imposed*, bureaucratic warehouse — the elder is *deposited*. The shift reveals modernity's commodification of care: love replaced by contract ("ukSdj"), duty by fee ("fuca/k"), family by institution. A student who says "both are for old people" fails to analyze the *agency* inversion. The text underscores this when ;'kksèkj ckcw notes: "xk¡o dk iq'rSuh ?kj VwV&iwQV pqdk gS" (a stranger's house is a temporary shelter) — the retirement home is not a chosen ashram but a waiting room for death.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The protagonist ;'kksèkj ckcw is passive — things happen *to* him; he never makes a real choice." Defend or refute using at least two decisions he *does* make in the opening sections.
questions.a: Refute. (1) He *chooses* to build the retirement home on his land — not for himself, but to preempt his children's guilt ("vki dks Hkh esjs thus osQ <ax ij dksbZ ,rjk"k gksuk ugha pkfg"). That is agency weaponized as sacrifice. (2) He *chooses* to hide his deteriorating health from fd'kunk ("og Hkh f"kíh ,slh gS fd bls gh igurh gS") — controlling information is a form of power. A student calling him "passive" confuses *quiet endurance* with *absence of will*. The text's tragedy is precisely that his choices are *moral*, not *self-serving* — and thus invisible to a transactional world.

questions.q: Write a 60-word diary entry from ;'kksèkj ckcw's perspective on the night he signs the retirement home papers, using the phrase "tks gqvk gksxk" exactly once — but *subverting* its usual resignation to show quiet defiance.
questions.a: A strong entry: "Signed the papers today. Children smiled — 'legkm baçkij' satisfied. They think I've surrendered. Let them. tks gqvk gksxk — but *I* decided where, when, and *whose* name goes on the gate. This home isn't my end. It's my witness." A weak entry treats "tks gqvk gksxk" as defeat ("I signed. tks gqvk gksxk. I am old."). The rubric: does the student grasp that the protagonist *reclaims* the phrase as a shield, not a shroud?
